questions.problem: Expressed as an improper fraction in lowest terms, $\frac{1}{4}+3-\frac{5}{8}=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

We add and subtract, from left to right:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}+3-\frac{5}{8} & = \\ (\frac{1}{4}+3)-\frac{5}{8} & = \\ (\frac{1}{4}+\frac{12}{4})-\frac{5}{8} & = \\ \frac{1+12}{4}-\frac{5}{8} & = \\ \frac{13}{4}-\frac{5}{8} & = \\ \frac{26}{8}-\frac{5}{8} & = \\ \frac{26-5}{8} & = \\ \frac{21}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Expressed as an improper fraction in lowest terms, $\frac{3}{7}÷\frac{2}{5}\times 7=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

We divide and multiply, from left to right:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{7}÷\frac{2}{5}\times 7 & = \\ (\frac{3}{7}÷\frac{2}{5})\times 7 & = \\ (\frac{3}{7}\times \frac{5}{2})\times 7 & = \\ \frac{3\times 5}{7\times 2}\times 7 & = \\ \frac{15}{14}\times 7 & = \\ \frac{15}{14}\times \frac{7}{1} & = \\ \frac{15\times 7}{14\times 1} & = \\ \frac{105}{14} & = \\ \frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Expressed as a fraction in lowest terms, $\frac{4}{3}÷2-\frac{1}{3}=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}÷2-\frac{1}{3} & = \\ (\frac{4}{3}÷\frac{2}{1})-\frac{1}{3} & = \\ (\frac{4}{3}\times \frac{1}{2})-\frac{1}{3} & = \\ (\frac{4\times 1}{3\times 2})-\frac{1}{3} & = \\ \frac{4}{6}-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{6}-\frac{1}{3} & = \\ \frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3} & = \\ \frac{2-1}{3} & = \\ \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}÷(7+5) & = \\ \frac{5}{2}÷12\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}÷12 & = \\ \frac{5}{2}÷\frac{12}{1} & = \\ \frac{5}{2}\times \frac{1}{12} & = \\ \frac{5\times 1}{2\times 12} & = \\ \frac{5}{24}\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating Expressions Containing Parentheses
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To evaluate this expression, we use PEMDAS.

First, we perform the operation inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3+6)÷\frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ 3÷\frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}3÷\frac{4}{3}-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ (3÷\frac{4}{3})-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ (\frac{3}{1}÷\frac{4}{3})-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ (\frac{3}{1}\times \frac{3}{4})-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ \frac{3\times 3}{1\times 4}-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ \frac{9}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we subtract:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{4}-\frac{1}{4} & = \\ \frac{9-1}{4} & = \\ \frac{8}{4} & = \\ 8÷4 & = \\ 2\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
As we already know, to evaluate numerical expressions with a mix of different operations, we must follow the order of operations known as PEMDAS.

The same rules apply to numerical expressions with negative numbers. For example, let's compute the value of

$$
\left( -5 + 7 \right) \div (-2) \times 6.
$$

First, we perform the operation inside the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-5+7)÷(-2)\times 6 & = \\ 2÷(-2)\times 6\end{aligned}
$$

Now recall that if both multiplication and division appear in an expression, we complete each operation from left to right (similarly for addition and subtraction).
So, we first divide:

$$
\begin{aligned}2÷(-2)\times 6 & = \\ -1\times 6\end{aligned}
$$

Then finally, we multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1\times 6 & =-6\end{aligned}
$$
